newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen rebel says Yeltsin health Russia's problem.
newsitem.headline: Chechen rebel says Yeltsin health Russia's problem.

text.p: Chechen separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev said on Friday that President Boris Yeltsin's health was a problem for Russia, not for Chechnya.
"We do not think Yeltsin's health can considerably influence the process of a peace settlement," Yandarbiyev said in an interview. "Russia does not need this war any more than Chechnya."
"If Yeltsin goes, it would be Russia's problem, not the problem of Chechnya. We are a sovereign state and do not want to interfere in these problems."

The bearded Yandarbiyev, in his traditional combat fatigues and Caucasian "papakha" lambswool hat, was commenting on Yeltsin's decision, announced on Thursday, to undergo heart surgery, probably later this month.
Yeltsin's envoy Alexander Lebed last Saturday signed a peace deal with the rebels under which the question of its future status was deferred for five years.

In December 1994, Yeltsin sent troops into Chechnya to quell its independence drive, but failed to achieve a decisive victory in 20 months of fighting in which tens of thousands of people died. The fighting abated after a truce last month.
On Friday, the separatists celebrate the fifth anniversary of their unilateral declaration of independence and Yandarbiyev made clear there could be no compromise on the cherished goal.

"Our independence exists from 1991, it has never ended," said Yandarbiyev, a poet who took over as the overall rebel leader in April after Dzhokhar Dudayev, who had led the independence drive, was killed in a rocket attack.
"Independence day is not a day of euphoria...It is not a day of victory...The war has not ended though we are making every effort to end it," Yandarbiyev said.
But he took a conciliatory line on how to proceed towards independence, saying he had every intention to honour the peace deal signed Lebed and rebel chief-of-staff Aslan Maskhadov.
"We trust Lebed we will adhere to the agreements we have reached. We expect Russia to respect its obligations as well."
The deal included a compromise on the future polical status of the mainly Moslem North Caucasus region by agreeing to put off a decision for five years.
The accord foresees the withdrawal of most of the troops, with Russian-Chechen joint patrols taking their place in the capital Grozny.

Some Russian hardliners see the actions of Lebed, hailed as a hero by the rebels, as outright capitulation. The difficulties ahead were underscored on Friday by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who had backed the peace accord.
"We have gathered Russia together for too long a time to give parts of it away now," Itar-Tass news agency quoted Chernomyrdin as saying in the Urals region of Orenburg.
Lebed returned to Moscow on Thursday after another round of talks with Maskhadov during which they agreed measures to build on the truce and the political deal.
Lebed said he and Maskhadov had agreed to make the capital Grozny a demilitarised zone in which only members of the joint patrols would be allowed to carry guns.
Yandarbiyev said on Friday he was ready to co-opt several ministers of the pro-Moscow Chechen administration into his government.
